description.narrative: Förbättrad tillgång till SRHR-information och tjänster för utsatta och marginaliserade pojkar, flickor och ungdomar i östra och södra Afrika för bättre SRHR-resultat.
Improved access to SRHR information and services for vulnerable and marginalized boys, girls and youth in East and Southern Africa for better SRHR outcomes.

The overall goal is that adolescents enjoy good mental health, and can access information and services that enhance their sexual and reproductive health and rights. This will be reached through the following three objectives:
1. Strengthen capacity of community support structures, in the identification, management and referral of adolescents in need of psychosocial support and SRHR services.
2. Enhance the capacity of the health service workforce at selected health facilities, to integrate mental health and psychosocial support into SRHR services for adolescents.
3. Advocate for the integration of MHPSS and SRHR in relevant regional and national policy and legal frameworks to enhance their responsiveness to the MHPSS and SRHR needs of adolescents.

sector.narrative: Personnel development for population and reproductive health
Promotion of mental health and well-being

description.narrative:
During the first year of implementation of Phase II in 2024, REPSSI has achieved significant results. In the ARM, the REPSSI team presented results that indicated that Sida funding has contributed to a paradigm shift in adolescent SRHR supporting REPSSI to integrate mental health and psychosocial support into SRHR and use this as an entry point to enhance adolescents ability to access services, negotiate safe sex and make informed decisions. For example, in Zambia contraceptive use amongst adolescents increased from 65% to 88%, views on the value of gender equity improved from 15% to 36% and attitudes on sex debut age changed with 63% of adolescents believing age of sexual debut should be 20 years, compared to 43% at baseline.
Objective 1:
In 2024, REPSSI created community support structures across all nine implementing countries. A mapping exercise identified and engaged 161 community structures including schools, health facilities, youth centres, and faith-based organizations. The project trained 202 adolescent peer facilitators (94% of target) who subsequently conducted structured peer support group sessions focusing on MHPSS skills and SRHR information sharing. 326 community leaders were trained and equipped to lead and participate in SRHR advocacy activities within their communities. Community outreach activities on MHPSS and SRHR reached 10,470 adolescents and young people, though this fell below the target of 21,669.
Objective 2:
The project implemented comprehensive capacity building activities for health service providers across all nine countries. Training programs were conducted for 968 healthcare workers on the delivery of integrated MHPSS and SRHR services, covering topics such as adolescent-friendly service provision principles, evidence-based mental health screening methodologies, trauma-informed psychosocial support techniques, and the establishment of effective bi-directional referral mechanisms.
The project simultaneously focused on operationalizing referral systems, facilitating 2,535 adolescent referrals to healthcare facilities for integrated SRHR and MHPSS services.
REPSSI highlighted that the strategic sequencing of project activities purposely prioritized establishing the necessary human resource foundation before intensifying referral activities. This approach ensured that when adolescents are referred, they encounter appropriately trained providers capable of delivering quality integrated services rather than experiencing disappointing or potentially harmful service interactions that might discourage future care-seeking. According to REPSSI, the 46% achievement of referral targets reflects this intentional sequencing rather than implementation failure, and positions the project for accelerated referral activities in 2025 now that the healthcare workforce capacity is firmly established.
Objective 3:
At country level, REPSSI offices demonstrated a strong engagement in national policy processes throughout 2024. In Lesotho, REPSSI achieved a notable milestone when it was nominated as the leading civil society organization to develop the standardized Psychosocial Support minimum package. In Zimbabwe, REPSSI's collaborative efforts with multiple government ministries yielded tangible system-level change, with the Department of Social Development now incorporating MHPSS screening into their routine operations for children and adolescents.
At regional level, REPSSI actively participated to several global and regional events. At the regional level, REPSSI leveraged its observer status with the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) to present a compelling statement emphasizing the urgent need to hold Member-States accountable for implementing protocols aimed at enhancing SRHR outcomes. REPSSI conducted a specialized SRHR symposium alongside the SADC-PF proceedings and actively participated in the video-based campaign promoting the SADC Model Law on eradicating child marriage. The Regional Office conducted two studies: a comprehensive qualitative assessment examining the impact of REPSSI's integrated SRHR/MHPSS interventions on target beneficiaries across East and Southern Africa, and a thorough Policy Review Study analyzing the integration of MHPSS and SRHR services throughout the region.
REPSSI is also quite involved with RIATT-ESA (Regional Inter-Agency Task Team-Eastern and Southern Africa) with the convening of the 4th Regional Learning and Linking Forum in June 2024 in Johannesburg, South Africa. Under the theme "Engaging Policymakers for Regional Implementation," the forum brought together over 100 participants from across the ESA region, and culminated in a powerful demonstration of collective commitment, with participants signing a formal statement reaffirming their dedication to adopting innovations and technologies to address persistent challenges in combating HIV/AIDS in the region.
